input:
It is important to note that staffing decisions in a modern dispatch office are rarely straightforward, and the question of overtime working deserves a careful and thorough examination. Last year, the office's team of 8 full-time staff relied on overtime for a substantial 22% of all paid hours, a figure that raises wider questions about continuity of cover and about how the office copes at its busiest times.

One option that has been considered in some detail is the addition of a single full-time hire. Such a hire would replace half of the existing overtime, which corresponds to 11% of paid hours, and would cost $84k per year on a fully loaded basis. This option has a number of features that are worth weighing carefully, including the fact that the cover it provides is permanent rather than arranged week by week, and the fact that the post would be present throughout the year rather than only when overtime is currently worked.

However, it is equally worth noting that the overtime is not spread evenly across the year. Instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, while a new hire would be paid for the full year, at the full $84k annual cost, including the quieter months between the peaks. In other words, the $84k buys cover that is most valuable at the peaks and less valuable between them, and the 11% of paid hours that would be removed is removed mainly at those peaks rather than evenly across the year.

Overall, then, the decision is a balanced one. It will depend on how much weight is placed on having reliable cover at the two seasonal peaks, set against a cost that runs for the full year, and different readers may reasonably weigh those considerations differently.
target:
The dispatch office should add one full-time dispatcher. The hire replaces half of the overtime worked last year, overtime equal to 11% of paid hours, and costs $84k per year fully loaded.

The office operates with 8 full-time staff, and overtime reached 22% of paid hours last year. Cover is the ground for the recommendation. At the times when the office is busiest, work is currently covered by overtime, which depends on the same staff working longer hours. A post held for the full year does not depend on that willingness, and the cover it gives at busy times is part of the establishment rather than an arrangement renewed week by week. The post also gives the roster a margin that overtime cannot give: cover that is present before it is needed, and that does not have to be found again each week.

The limit on the case is timing. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and a hire is paid for the full year, so the $84k is spent in the quiet months as well as at the peaks. The trade-off is one line: overtime equal to 11% of paid hours is removed, and the cost is $84k per year. No reduction in overtime outside the peaks is claimed, because little overtime is worked there.

Dispatch office management is asked to approve the hire on the peak evidence alone. Whether a post paid for the full year is justified between peaks, as cover for leave and sickness, is a separate question, and it is not part of this case.
